claim: Current databases hold hundreds of millions of human single-nucleotide variants.
source: As a consequence of stunning technological advances – especially in DNA-sequencing – current databases hold hundreds of millions of human single-nucleotide variants, with nearly 5 million in the tiny portion of the genome that encodes protein sequence (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 which shows variant data, and is stated as a factual observation about current databases.

claim: Nearly 5 million single-nucleotide variants exist in the portion of the genome that encodes protein sequence.
source: As a consequence of stunning technological advances – especially in DNA-sequencing – current databases hold hundreds of millions of human single-nucleotide variants, with nearly 5 million in the tiny portion of the genome that encodes protein sequence (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and stated as a factual observation about variant databases.

claim: Only about 2% of amino acid replacement variants have been clinically interpreted.
source: Yet our knowledge of the functional effects of all this variation is vanishingly small: even for the changes that result in amino acid replacements, only about 2% have been clinically interpreted, and about 80% of those have been interpreted as 'variants of uncertain significance' (Fayer et al., 2021; Starita et al., 2017; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fayer et al., 2021 and Starita et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1.

claim: About 80% of clinically interpreted amino acid replacement variants have been interpreted as 'variants of uncertain significance'.
source: Yet our knowledge of the functional effects of all this variation is vanishingly small: even for the changes that result in amino acid replacements, only about 2% have been clinically interpreted, and about 80% of those have been interpreted as 'variants of uncertain significance' (Fayer et al., 2021; Starita et al., 2017; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fayer et al., 2021 and Starita et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Breaking through the interpretative bottleneck of variant effects constitutes a central challenge for human genomics research.
source: Breaking through this interpretative bottleneck constitutes a central challenge for human genomics research.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of the field based on the preceding discussion of limited variant interpretation.

claim: Multiplex assays of variant effect (MAVEs) experimentally assess the effects of single-nucleotide variants at scale.
source: Multiplex assays of variant effect (MAVEs) experimentally assess the effects of single-nucleotide variants at scale.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about MAVEs that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In MAVEs, a single open-reading frame, exon, or regulatory region is saturated with all possible single-nucleotide changes.
source: Here, a single open-reading frame, exon, or regulatory region is saturated with all possible single-nucleotide changes, and a single property is measured via coupling this property to the number of DNA sequence reads of each variant before and after a functional selection (Esposito et al., 2019; Findlay, 2021; Kinney and McCandlish, 2019; Starita et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing MAVE methodology.

claim: MAVEs measure a single property via coupling this property to the number of DNA sequence reads of each variant before and after a functional selection.
source: Here, a single open-reading frame, exon, or regulatory region is saturated with all possible single-nucleotide changes, and a single property is measured via coupling this property to the number of DNA sequence reads of each variant before and after a functional selection (Esposito et al., 2019; Findlay, 2021; Kinney and McCandlish, 2019; Starita et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing MAVE methodology.

claim: Functional data from MAVEs can reveal whether and how each variant alters function.
source: We and others have shown that the resulting functional data can reveal whether and how each variant alters function, and that the functional data empower the interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (Fayer et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2022; Starita et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2016; Tabet et al., 2022; Weile et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating this capability.

claim: Functional data from MAVEs empower the interpretation of variants of uncertain significance.
source: We and others have shown that the resulting functional data can reveal whether and how each variant alters function, and that the functional data empower the interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (Fayer et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2022; Starita et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2016; Tabet et al., 2022; Weile et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating this capability.

claim: Integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~70% of variants of uncertain significance in TP53.
source: For example, the integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~70% of variants of uncertain significance in TP53, ~50% in BRCA1, and ~15% in PTEN (Fayer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fayer et al., 2021 which provides the data.

claim: Integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~50% of variants of uncertain significance in BRCA1.
source: For example, the integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~70% of variants of uncertain significance in TP53, ~50% in BRCA1, and ~15% in PTEN (Fayer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fayer et al., 2021 which provides the data.

claim: Integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~15% of variants of uncertain significance in PTEN.
source: For example, the integration of multiplex functional data for cancer-related genes led to the reinterpretation of ~70% of variants of uncertain significance in TP53, ~50% in BRCA1, and ~15% in PTEN (Fayer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fayer et al., 2021 which provides the data.

claim: The first generation of MAVEs is being deployed widely.
source: Spurred on by these and other results, the first generation of MAVEs is being deployed widely (Da et al., 2021; Esposito et al., 2019; Fowler et al., 2021; Rubin et al., 2021), and comprehensive variant effect maps for easy-to-measure cellular properties, such as growth, are within reach for many clinically relevant human genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the deployment of MAVEs.

claim: Comprehensive variant effect maps for easy-to-measure cellular properties, such as growth, are within reach for many clinically relevant human genes.
source: Spurred on by these and other results, the first generation of MAVEs is being deployed widely (Da et al., 2021; Esposito et al., 2019; Fowler et al., 2021; Rubin et al., 2021), and comprehensive variant effect maps for easy-to-measure cellular properties, such as growth, are within reach for many clinically relevant human genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of MAVE technology and its deployment.

claim: MAVEs have not been extended to structural variation, copy number variation in repetitive DNA, and other large and complex variants.
source: For one, MAVEs have not been extended to structural variation, copy number variation in repetitive DNA, and other large and complex variants that are likely numerous and highly impactful (Manolio et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2021; Mitra et al., 2021; Press et al., 2014; Press et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitations of MAVEs, with citations supporting the importance of these variant types.

claim: Structural variation, copy number variation in repetitive DNA, and other large and complex variants are likely numerous and highly impactful.
source: For one, MAVEs have not been extended to structural variation, copy number variation in repetitive DNA, and other large and complex variants that are likely numerous and highly impactful (Manolio et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2021; Mitra et al., 2021; Press et al., 2014; Press et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the importance of these variant types.

claim: New experimental and computational approaches are needed to make complex variation accessible for phenotyping in high throughput.
source: To make such complex variation accessible for phenotyping in high throughput, new experimental and computational approaches are needed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current limitations of MAVE technology.

claim: Existing MAVEs generally do not account for genetic, environmental, or tissue/developmental context.
source: Yet even for single-nucleotide variants for which MAVEs exist or can be envisioned, major challenges for accurate variant effect interpretation remain. Existing MAVEs generally do not account for genetic, environmental, or tissue/developmental context (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the current limitations of MAVEs, with reference to Figure 2 illustrating these contexts.

claim: Assessing and perturbing context is essential for fully characterizing the effect of a genetic variant.
source: Assessing and perturbing this context is essential for fully characterizing the effect of a genetic variant (Claussnitzer and Susztak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Claussnitzer and Susztak, 2021.

claim: The lack of context in MAVEs constrains their utility for understanding how variants interact with genetic background.
source: This lack of context constrains the utility of MAVEs for understanding how variants interact with genetic background, affect non cell-autonomous phenotypes, and alter organismal phenotype in interplay with environmental factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current MAVE approaches.

claim: The lack of context in MAVEs constrains their utility for understanding how variants affect non cell-autonomous phenotypes.
source: This lack of context constrains the utility of MAVEs for understanding how variants interact with genetic background, affect non cell-autonomous phenotypes, and alter organismal phenotype in interplay with environmental factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current MAVE approaches.

claim: The lack of context in MAVEs constrains their utility for understanding how variants alter organismal phenotype in interplay with environmental factors.
source: This lack of context constrains the utility of MAVEs for understanding how variants interact with genetic background, affect non cell-autonomous phenotypes, and alter organismal phenotype in interplay with environmental factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current MAVE approaches.

claim: Onset, severity, and incidence of disease can differ widely among carriers of a given disease-associated variant.
source: Onset, severity, and even incidence of disease can differ widely among carriers of a given disease-associated variant.
evidence: This is established knowledge about variable expressivity and penetrance of genetic variants.

claim: Small and moderate effect variants associated with common diseases through GWAS show particularly wide differences in disease onset, severity, and incidence among carriers.
source: This is particularly true for small and moderate effect variants that are associated with common diseases through genome-wide association studies (GWAS).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about GWAS variants.

claim: The heritability explained by GWAS variants tends to be small.
source: The heritability explained by GWAS variants tends to be small, and these variants typically have little power to predict the disease risk of individuals (Eichler et al., 2010; Gibson, 2012; Khera et al., 2018; Manolio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting this phenomenon.

claim: GWAS variants typically have little power to predict the disease risk of individuals.
source: The heritability explained by GWAS variants tends to be small, and these variants typically have little power to predict the disease risk of individuals (Eichler et al., 2010; Gibson, 2012; Khera et al., 2018; Manolio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting this phenomenon.

claim: The 'missing heritability' of common diseases is commonly attributed to uncharacterized non-additive genetic interactions.
source: This 'missing heritability' of common diseases and the differences in variant expressivity among patients with highly penetrant, rare Mendelian disorders are commonly attributed to uncharacterized non-additive genetic interactions, among other factors (Eichler et al., 2010; Gibson, 2012; Manolio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations discussing missing heritability.

claim: Differences in variant expressivity among patients with highly penetrant, rare Mendelian disorders are commonly attributed to uncharacterized non-additive genetic interactions.
source: This 'missing heritability' of common diseases and the differences in variant expressivity among patients with highly penetrant, rare Mendelian disorders are commonly attributed to uncharacterized non-additive genetic interactions, among other factors (Eichler et al., 2010; Gibson, 2012; Manolio et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations discussing variable expressivity.

claim: Non-additive genetic interaction, or epistasis, describes the phenomenon that the combined effect of alleles at two or more loci deviates from the sum of their individual effects.
source: Non-additive genetic interaction, or epistasis, describes the phenomenon that the combined effect of alleles at two or more loci deviates from the sum of their individual effects (Fisher, 1919; Mackay, 2001).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by foundational citations.

claim: The importance of non-additive genetic interactions, particularly for complex traits, has been the subject of a long-standing debate.
source: The importance of non-additive genetic interactions, in particular for complex traits, has been the subject of a long-standing debate (Fisher, 1930; Hivert et al., 2021; Wade and Goodnight, 1998; Wright, 1931), and the importance of epistasis across the allele frequency spectrum is not well understood.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations spanning nearly a century of debate.

claim: The importance of epistasis across the allele frequency spectrum is not well understood.
source: The importance of non-additive genetic interactions, in particular for complex traits, has been the subject of a long-standing debate (Fisher, 1930; Hivert et al., 2021; Wade and Goodnight, 1998; Wright, 1931), and the importance of epistasis across the allele frequency spectrum is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Model organism research has identified many examples of non-additive genetic interactions affecting a wide variety of morphological and quantitative traits in fungi, animals, and plants.
source: Model organism research has identified many examples of non-additive genetic interactions affecting a wide variety of morphological and quantitative traits in fungi, animals, and plants (Costanzo et al., 2019; Forsberg et al., 2017; Mackay, 2014; Press et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting epistasis in model organisms.

claim: Genetic interactions often reflect functional relationships such as those among genes coding for subunits of a multimeric protein complex or proteins functioning in a common pathway.
source: These genetic interactions often reflect functional relationships such as those among genes coding for subunits of a multimeric protein complex or proteins functioning in a common pathway (Costanzo et al., 2019; Miller and Piccolo, 2020; Narasimhan et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2017; Pamplona-Cunha et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting functional relationships underlying epistasis.

claim: Quantitative genetics theory and empirical data for human and crop traits show that additive genetic models can explain over half of the total genetic contributions to complex traits.
source: Quantitative genetics theory and empirical data for human and crop traits show that additive genetic models can explain over half of the total genetic contributions to complex traits (Darnell et al., 2022; Dudley, 2007; Hivert et al., 2021; Sheppard et al., 2021; Visscher et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations providing theoretical and empirical evidence.

claim: Accounting for non-additive genetic effects, particularly epistatic interactions, can lead to more accurate phenotype predictions.
source: However, accounting for non-additive genetic effects, and particularly epistatic interactions, can lead to more accurate phenotype predictions (Carlborg et al., 2006; Forsberg et al., 2017; Lachowiec et al., 2015; Matsui et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations demonstrating improved prediction with epistasis.

claim: Methods that examine genetic ancestry and portability can improve prediction and estimation in the presence of non-additive genetic effects.
source: Methods that examine genetic ancestry and portability can also improve prediction and estimation in the presence of these effects (Brown, 2016; Park et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting these methods.

claim: A large majority of disease-associated GWAS variants reside within or in linkage with accessible chromatin regions.
source: Because a large majority of disease-associated GWAS variants reside within or in linkage with accessible chromatin regions, complex diseases are assumed to arise through the additive action of many regulatory variants (Maurano et al., 2012; Meuleman et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations documenting the enrichment of GWAS variants in regulatory regions.

claim: Complex diseases are assumed to arise through the additive action of many regulatory variants.
source: Because a large majority of disease-associated GWAS variants reside within or in linkage with accessible chromatin regions, complex diseases are assumed to arise through the additive action of many regulatory variants (Maurano et al., 2012; Meuleman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of GWAS variants in regulatory regions, supported by citations.

claim: The Omnigenic model posits that 'core genes', which are functionally related to a phenotype of interest, carry common, small-effect, significantly trait-associated variants that together contribute little to heritability.
source: This theoretical framework posits that 'core genes', which are functionally related to a phenotype of interest, carry common, small-effect, significantly trait-associated variants that together contribute little to heritability while the bulk of heritability is contributed by a huge number of common 'peripheral' variants with individually tiny effects that ultimately affect core gene expression.
evidence: This is a description of the Omnigenic model theoretical framework.

claim: The Omnigenic model posits that the bulk of heritability is contributed by a huge number of common 'peripheral' variants with individually tiny effects that ultimately affect core gene expression.
source: This theoretical framework posits that 'core genes', which are functionally related to a phenotype of interest, carry common, small-effect, significantly trait-associated variants that together contribute little to heritability while the bulk of heritability is contributed by a huge number of common 'peripheral' variants with individually tiny effects that ultimately affect core gene expression.
evidence: This is a description of the Omnigenic model theoretical framework.

claim: In the Omnigenic model, peripheral variants are uniformly distributed over the genome, with each chromosome contributing to trait heritability according to its size.
source: Peripheral variants are uniformly distributed over the genome, with each chromosome contributing to trait heritability according to its size, reminiscent of Fisher's Infinitesimal model (Barton et al., 2017; Walsh and Lynch, 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the Omnigenic model with citation to related theoretical work.

claim: The Omnigenic model is not universally accepted.
source: The Omnigenic model is not universally accepted (Connally et al., 2022; Sohail et al., 2019), but it offers an explanation for the missing heritability conundrum and is supported by recent empirical studies (Sinnott-Armstrong et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to critiques of the model.

claim: The Omnigenic model offers an explanation for the missing heritability conundrum.
source: The Omnigenic model is not universally accepted (Connally et al., 2022; Sohail et al., 2019), but it offers an explanation for the missing heritability conundrum and is supported by recent empirical studies (Sinnott-Armstrong et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical contribution of the Omnigenic model.

claim: The Omnigenic model is supported by recent empirical studies.
source: The Omnigenic model is not universally accepted (Connally et al., 2022; Sohail et al., 2019), but it offers an explanation for the missing heritability conundrum and is supported by recent empirical studies (Sinnott-Armstrong et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: There are many recessive variants of unknown molecular or cellular functional consequence in disease-associated genes.
source: There are many recessive variants of unknown molecular or cellular functional consequence in disease-associated genes, even amongst the thousands of genes that play a role in highly penetrant Mendelian disorders.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding recessive variants.

claim: Individuals can carry different alleles of a gene that together as a compound heterozygote alter gene activity enough to cause disease.
source: Examples abound of cases in which individuals carry different alleles of a gene that together – as a compound heterozygote – alter gene activity enough to cause disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about compound heterozygosity in genetic disease.

claim: Compound heterozygote alleles may act additively or non-additively, enabling valuable mechanistic insights on disease origins.
source: These alleles may act additively or non-additively, enabling valuable mechanistic insights on disease origins, a first crucial step toward future therapy.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of studying compound heterozygotes.

claim: Assaying combinations of common, disease-associated GWAS variants with all possible other variants in the same gene and regulatory region is a promising approach.
source: Another promising approach is assaying combinations of common, disease-associated GWAS variants with all possible other variants in the same gene and regulatory region (Figure 2B), a likely scenario by which the penetrance and expressivity of a common variant may be altered.
evidence: This is a proposed approach based on inference about how variant effects may be modified.

claim: Variants of a given gene or regulatory region will need to be assessed in pairwise fashion to address compound heterozygotes and combinations of GWAS variants with rare variants.
source: To address both of these scenarios, variants of a given gene or regulatory region will need to be assessed in pairwise fashion.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental requirements for studying variant combinations.

claim: Executing pairwise variant experiments in human cells across all possible variant pairs will require innovation in variant barcoding, genome engineering, and sequencing strategies.
source: Executing such experiments in human cells across all possible variant pairs will require some innovation in variant barcoding, genome engineering, and sequencing strategies to unambiguously link both variants with a cell's phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference about the technical requirements for proposed experiments.

claim: Systematic evaluation of compound heterozygotes and combinations of GWAS variants with rare variants affecting the same locus will yield actionable information for genetic counselors, physicians and patients.
source: However, the systematic evaluation of compound heterozygotes and of combinations of GWAS variants with rare variants affecting the same locus will yield actionable information for genetic counselors, physicians and patients.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential clinical utility of proposed experiments.

claim: Experimentally addressing the consequences of more complex genetic interactions will require sophisticated technological innovations and novel data analysis methods.
source: Experimentally addressing the consequences of more complex genetic interactions (Figure 2B) will require sophisticated technological innovations and novel data analysis methods.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for studying complex genetic interactions.

claim: Variant libraries could be introduced into many different cell lines, including iPSCs derived from diverse individuals, to test the consequences and interactions of many different genetic variants.
source: For example, variant libraries could be introduced into many different cell lines, including induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from diverse individuals, thereby testing the consequences and interactions of many different genetic variants, including structural variants.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental approach.

claim: Identifying causal additive or non-additive genetic interactions from variant libraries in diverse cell lines will be a formidable challenge.
source: Identifying causal additive or non-additive genetic interactions in this scenario will be a formidable challenge.
evidence: This is an inference about the difficulty of the proposed approach.

claim: Variant libraries could be introduced into cells carrying programmed genetic perturbations such as gene deletion, knockdown, or overexpression.
source: Alternatively, variant libraries could be introduced into cells carrying programmed genetic perturbations such as gene deletion, knockdown, or overexpression.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental approach.

claim: Variant libraries for a disease-associated core gene could be introduced into cell lines carrying common variants in other core genes for the same trait to test assumptions of the Omnigenic model empirically.
source: Most ambitious, variant libraries for a disease-associated core gene could be introduced into cell lines carrying common variants in other core genes for the same trait, testing some assumptions of the Omnigenic model empirically.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental approach to test a theoretical model.

claim: If variant effect mapping were possible in whole animals, genetic crosses and high-throughput phenotyping could be used to interrogate the phenotypes of many different combinations of variant libraries.
source: If it were possible to conduct variant effect mapping in whole animals, genetic crosses and high-throughput phenotyping could be used to interrogate the phenotypes of many different combinations of variant libraries with each other, other variant libraries, or possible modifier loci.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential experimental approaches.

claim: Experimental efforts to study genetic context must go hand in hand with innovative theoretical studies to enable predictions of variant effects in genetic context.
source: Most importantly, these experimental efforts must go hand in hand with innovative theoretical studies to enable predictions of variant effects in genetic context.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on inference about the requirements for understanding variant effects.

claim: Combining existing variant effect maps of disease-associated genes with genome-wide polygenic risk scores is one approach to investigate the Omnigenic model.
source: For example, combining existing variant effect maps of disease-associated genes with genome-wide polygenic risk scores is one approach to investigate the Omnigenic model.
evidence: This is a proposed computational approach.

claim: Combining variant effect maps with polygenic risk scores could leverage biobanks and human phenotype data to identify modifier loci and refine variant effect maps.
source: Such a modeling approach could leverage the growing resources of biobanks and human phenotype data to identify modifier loci and refine variant effect maps (Schiabor Barrett et al., 2022; Tabet et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of a proposed approach, with citations to related work.

claim: Loci that are significantly associated with different disorders represent candidates for genetic modifiers that alter the penetrance and expressivity of other variants.
source: Similarly, taking advantage of the multitude of high-quality GWAS, one could systematically explore loci that are significantly associated with different disorders; these loci represent candidates for genetic modifiers that alter the penetrance and expressivity of other variants (Lehner et al., 2006; Queitsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed approach with citations to supporting concepts.

claim: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is a known genetic modifier locus.
source: One such locus is known: the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), which encodes cell surface proteins that are essential for the adaptive immune system by virtue of their ability to 'display' a cell's repertoire of contained peptides to the immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the MHC.

claim: The MHC encodes cell surface proteins that are essential for the adaptive immune system by virtue of their ability to 'display' a cell's repertoire of contained peptides to the immune system.
source: One such locus is known: the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), which encodes cell surface proteins that are essential for the adaptive immune system by virtue of their ability to 'display' a cell's repertoire of contained peptides to the immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC function.

claim: Different MHC alleles display different sets of variant peptides, offering avenues for MHC variation to alter the penetrance and expressivity of many other variants.
source: The fact that different MHC alleles display different sets of variant peptides offers avenues for MHC variation to alter the penetrance and expressivity of many other variants.
evidence: This is an inference based on known MHC biology.

claim: Stratifying existing GWAS by outliers, focusing on individuals with the most and least severe disease phenotypes, might identify genetic modifiers of variant penetrance and expressivity.
source: Stratifying existing GWAS by outliers, for example, focusing on individuals with the most and least severe disease phenotypes, might also identify genetic modifiers of variant penetrance and expressivity, where they exist (Gibson, 2009; Lehner et al., 2006; Queitsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed approach with citations to supporting concepts.

claim: There is limited evidence for dominance in human genotype–phenotype mapping.
source: Although there is limited evidence for dominance in human genotype–phenotype mapping and epistasis remains difficult to quantify genome-wide thus far, we anticipate that understanding epistatic effects at individual genes will yield valuable insight into the extent of these epistatic interactions and their phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of evidence in the field.

claim: Epistasis remains difficult to quantify genome-wide.
source: Although there is limited evidence for dominance in human genotype–phenotype mapping and epistasis remains difficult to quantify genome-wide thus far, we anticipate that understanding epistatic effects at individual genes will yield valuable insight into the extent of these epistatic interactions and their phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Understanding epistatic effects at individual genes will yield valuable insight into the extent of epistatic interactions and their phenotypic consequences.
source: Although there is limited evidence for dominance in human genotype–phenotype mapping and epistasis remains difficult to quantify genome-wide thus far, we anticipate that understanding epistatic effects at individual genes will yield valuable insight into the extent of these epistatic interactions and their phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the anticipated value of studying epistasis at individual genes.

claim: Variants in some genes affect all cell types similarly across development.
source: Although variants in some genes affect all cell types similarly across development, variants more often exert their effect in specific tissues, and at specific stages of development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about variant effects.

claim: Variants more often exert their effect in specific tissues and at specific stages of development.
source: Although variants in some genes affect all cell types similarly across development, variants more often exert their effect in specific tissues, and at specific stages of development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about variant effects.

claim: Pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes confer a greatly increased risk of some, but not all, types of cancer.
source: For example, pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which play a fundamental role in DNA repair, confer a greatly increased risk of some, but not all, types of cancer (Welcsh and King, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Welcsh and King, 2001.

claim: BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes play a fundamental role in DNA repair.
source: For example, pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which play a fundamental role in DNA repair, confer a greatly increased risk of some, but not all, types of cancer (Welcsh and King, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BRCA1/2 function.

claim: Variants affecting metabolic or neurodevelopmental disorders like atypical pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration and schizophrenia can show effects in specific tissues and/or developmental stages.
source: Variants affecting metabolic or neurodevelopmental disorders like atypical pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration and schizophrenia can show effects in specific tissues and/or developmental stages (Immonen et al., 2017; Kurian and Hayflick, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies of these disorders.

claim: Different variants in the same gene can affect different tissues and cause different diseases.
source: Moreover, different variants in the same gene can affect different tissues and cause different diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about variant effects.

claim: Pathogenic germline variants in LMNA most often cause cardiomyopathy, but can also cause muscular dystrophy, lipodystrophy, or the premature aging syndrome progeria.
source: For example, pathogenic germline variants in LMNA most often cause cardiomyopathy, but can also cause muscular dystrophy, lipodystrophy, or the premature aging syndrome progeria (Novelli and D'Apice, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Novelli and D'Apice, 2003.

claim: Regulatory variants at a given locus can have pleiotropic effects on tissue specificity because enhancer elements are able to activate multiple genes.
source: This complexity only expands with regulatory variants at a given locus, where enhancer elements are able to activate multiple genes (Hu and Tee, 2017), causing pleiotropic effects on tissue specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and inference about regulatory variant effects.

claim: Recent approaches have dramatically improved the linkage of regulatory variants to target genes.
source: While recent approaches have dramatically improved the linkage of regulatory variants to target genes (Andersson et al., 2014; Dey et al., 2022; Gschwind et al., 2023; Nasser et al., 2021; Kundaje et al., 2015), this remains an area of substantial ongoing work.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: Linking regulatory variants to target genes remains an area of substantial ongoing work.
source: While recent approaches have dramatically improved the linkage of regulatory variants to target genes (Andersson et al., 2014; Dey et al., 2022; Gschwind et al., 2023; Nasser et al., 2021; Kundaje et al., 2015), this remains an area of substantial ongoing work.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Numerous existing studies have begun to tackle the application of MAVE technologies to regulatory regions.
source: Even so, numerous existing studies have begun to tackle the application of MAVE technologies to regulatory regions (Gasperini et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2020; Kircher et al., 2019; Klein et al., 2018; Morova et al., 2023; Vockley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies applying MAVEs to regulatory regions.

claim: Regulatory region MAVEs rely on the same assumptions as coding variant MAVEs, namely that there is a direct link to the phenotype being selected and that variants have variable effects on that phenotype in the cell type being screened.
source: These studies rely on the same assumptions as coding variant MAVEs, namely that there is a direct link to the phenotype being selected and that variants have variable effects on that phenotype in the cell type being screened.

claim: The relative importance of external versus internal cellular environments is much debated.
source: In addition to variant effect mapping across a range of external conditions, the internal conditions of the cells and organisms carrying variants can be drastically changed. The relative importance of external versus internal cellular environments is much debated (Billman, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work discussing this debate.

claim: An approach to induce mistranslation across the entire proteome for a given codon can manipulate internal cellular environments and allow their effects on individual variants to be measured.
source: Here, an approach to induce mistranslation across the entire proteome for a given codon (Berg et al., 2019; Cozma et al., 2022) can manipulate internal cellular environments and allow their effects on individual variants to be measured.
evidence: This is a proposed approach with citations to supporting technology.

claim: One may consider manipulating splicing, protein folding, protein turnover, or mitochondrial function as general measures to affect cellular environment as it occurs in human aging.
source: Similarly, one may consider manipulating splicing, protein folding, protein turnover, or mitochondrial function as general measures to affect cellular environment as it occurs in human aging (Johnson et al., 1999; Leutert et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a proposed approach with citations to supporting concepts.

claim: Pharmacological perturbation of key cellular processes could be applied to alter cell–cell interactions and niche formation to understand intra-organismal effects of genetic variants.
source: Analogously, pharmacological perturbation of key cellular processes could be applied to alter cell–cell interactions and niche formation to understand intra-organismal (i.e., organism-autonomous) effects of genetic variants.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental approach.

claim: Quantifying gene–environment effects on an organismal trait must consider prior knowledge of variant effects on gene function, the consequences of perturbed gene function on cellular function within the context of the whole organism, and an organism's environmental exposures.
source: Quantifying gene–environment effects on an organismal trait must consider prior knowledge of variant effects on gene function, the consequences of perturbed gene function on cellular function within the context of the whole organism, and an organism's environmental exposures (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for quantifying gene-environment effects.

claim: Multiple unknown factors in gene-environment effects are difficult to disentangle without acquiring knowledge of each component, but data from MAVEs enable systematic disentanglement.
source: These multiple unknown factors are difficult to disentangle without acquiring knowledge of each component, but data from MAVEs enable us to do so systematically.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of MAVEs for understanding gene-environment effects.

claim: Gene–environment interactions will affect an organismal trait at the level of genes, cells, tissues, and whole organisms.
source: Similar to pleiotropy (Solovieff et al., 2013), gene–environment interactions will affect an organismal trait at the level of genes, cells, tissues, and whole organisms (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference about the multi-level nature of gene-environment effects, with citation to related concept.

claim: Under the simplifying assumption that most genetic effects are due to variants acting on genes or their products, variant effects on a trait can be separated into the contribution of that variant to the target gene and the effect of that gene on the trait of interest.
source: Under the simplifying assumption that most genetic effects are due to variants acting on genes or their products, we can separate variant effects on a trait into two components, the contribution of that variant to the target gene and the effect of that gene on the trait of interest (Mostafavi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a modeling framework with citation to supporting work.

claim: Incorporating environmental context into the two-component model of variant effects makes it substantially more complicated, but more reflective of biological reality, and hence more predictive of variant effects and disease risks.
source: Incorporating environmental context into this model makes it substantially more complicated, but more reflective of biological reality, and hence more predictive of variant effects and disease risks (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the value of incorporating environmental context into models.

claim: The scale and highly controlled nature of MAVE-derived variant effects will make it possible to disentangle the contributions of environmental interactions from variant-to-gene and gene-to-trait components.
source: The scale and highly controlled nature of MAVE-derived variant effects will make it possible to disentangle the contributions of environmental interactions from the two components as defined above.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the utility of MAVEs for understanding gene-environment effects.

claim: In the clinic, the individual matters because each person has their private set of common and rare variants and unique environmental exposures that together determine disease risk and prognosis.
source: In the clinic, the individual matters. Each of us has our private set of common and rare variants and our unique environmental exposures that together determine our disease risk and prognosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of individual variation for clinical medicine.

claim: MAVEs in genetic, developmental, and environmental contexts will allow a systematic characterization of the relative importance of each context for variant effect.
source: We argue that MAVEs in genetic, developmental, and environmental contexts will allow a systematic characterization of the relative importance of each context for variant effect as well as the characterization of variants particularly impacted by a given context or context combination.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of contextual MAVEs.

claim: MAVEs in genetic, developmental, and environmental contexts will allow characterization of variants particularly impacted by a given context or context combination.
source: We argue that MAVEs in genetic, developmental, and environmental contexts will allow a systematic characterization of the relative importance of each context for variant effect as well as the characterization of variants particularly impacted by a given context or context combination.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of contextual MAVEs.

claim: As MAVEs that can measure phenotypes more complex than cell survival or cell fitness are deployed widely, we will begin to gather mechanistic insight on variant function at large scale and in response to multiple environmental perturbations.
source: Moreover, as MAVEs that can measure phenotypes more complex than cell survival or cell fitness are deployed widely, we will begin to gather mechanistic insight on variant function at large scale and in response to multiple environmental perturbations.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future of MAVEs.

claim: Current approaches to decipher biological mechanisms of specific variants through variant-to-function analyses remain laborious and highly specialized.
source: Current approaches to decipher biological mechanisms of specific variants through variant-to-function analyses remain laborious and highly specialized (Claussnitzer and Susztak, 2021; Tabet et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to work on variant-to-function analyses.

claim: Conducting MAVEs in context offers the promise of scale and systematic analysis for deciphering biological mechanisms.
source: As we must pursue mechanistic insights into variant effects to separate confounding from causal association, conducting MAVEs in context offers the promise of scale and systematic analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of contextual MAVEs.

claim: The more contextual multiplex variant functional data becomes available, the more modeling approaches like machine learning and artificial intelligence can be used to infer variant-specific and context-dependent biological mechanisms.
source: The more contextual multiplex variant functional data becomes available, the more modeling approaches that rely on vast datasets such as machine learning and artificial intelligence can be used to infer variant-specific and context-dependent biological mechanisms, thereby informing individualized predictions of disease risk for rare and common diseases and facilitating their prevention and treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future applications of contextual MAVE data.

claim: Inferring variant-specific and context-dependent biological mechanisms will inform individualized predictions of disease risk for rare and common diseases and facilitate their prevention and treatment.
source: The more contextual multiplex variant functional data becomes available, the more modeling approaches that rely on vast datasets such as machine learning and artificial intelligence can be used to infer variant-specific and context-dependent biological mechanisms, thereby informing individualized predictions of disease risk for rare and common diseases and facilitating their prevention and treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the clinical applications of understanding variant mechanisms.

claim: A key question is which genes and regulatory regions are most likely to yield the most useful information for precision medicine and should be the focus of MAVEs in context.
source: A key question is which genes and regulatory regions are most likely to yield the most useful information for precision medicine, and therefore should be the focus of MAVEs in context.
evidence: This is a statement about priorities for future research.

claim: A simple answer for prioritizing genes for MAVEs is to focus on genes that contain many variants of uncertain significance and that are actionable with existing prevention and treatment options.
source: A simple answer is to focus on the genes that contain many variants of uncertain significance and that are actionable with existing prevention and treatment options.
evidence: This is a proposed prioritization strategy.

claim: Focusing only on genes with many VUS and existing treatment options will exclude many regulatory and coding GWAS variants associated with common disease for which context will likely matter the most.
source: This approach, however, will exclude many of the regulatory and coding GWAS variants associated with common disease for which context, in particular environmental context, will likely matter the most.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of a proposed prioritization strategy.

claim: To understand complex common diseases, experimentalists and theoreticians will need to come together to innovate and develop strategies to study human variants at genome scale and in multiple contexts.
source: If we are to understand complex common diseases, experimentalists and theoreticians will need to come together to innovate and develop strategies to study human variants at genome scale and in multiple contexts.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research directions.

claim: Figure 2B shows that gene–gene interactions are examined in different models at different levels of phenotype complexity.
source: (B) Gene–gene interactions are examined in different models at different levels of phenotype complexity.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 2B describing what the figure shows.

claim: Figure 2B suggests that gene–gene interactions for prioritization include compound heterozygotes, combinations of common and rare variants in a given locus in cis and trans, and experiments testing variants on different genetic backgrounds.
source: Gene–gene interactions suggested for prioritization include compound heterozygotes, combinations of common and rare variants in a given locus in cis and trans, and experiments testing variants on different genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 2B describing what the figure shows.

claim: Figure 2C shows that gene–environment interactions are examined at different levels of phenotype complexity.
source: (C) Gene–environment interactions are examined at different levels of phenotype complexity.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 2C describing what the figure shows.

claim: Figure 2C suggests three broad categories to model the complexity of environmental context in the laboratory: abiotic stress, challenges to immunity, and metabolism.
source: Three broad categories are suggested to model the complexity of environmental context in the laboratory: abiotic stress, challenges to immunity, and metabolism.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 2C describing what the figure shows.

claim: Figure 3B illustrates that gene–environment interactions affect an organismal trait at the level of genes, cells, tissues, and whole organisms.
source: (B) Gene–environment interactions will affect an organismal trait at the level of genes, cells, tissues, and whole organisms.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 3B describing what the figure illustrates.

claim: Figure 3B shows that extending the Mostafavi et al., 2022 model to incorporate environmental context captures more relevant biology and facilitates variant effect interpretation.
source: Extending the Mostafavi et al., 2022 model to incorporate environmental context captures more relevant biology, and hence facilitates variant effect interpretation.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 3B describing the model shown.

claim: Figure 3B illustrates that in the example shown, environmental context determines the trait value (obesity) for mice carrying a particular variant.
source: In the example shown, environmental context determines the trait value (obesity, big light-gray mouse) for mice carrying the red variant.
evidence: This is part of the caption for Figure 3B describing the example illustrated.
